vasopressin therapy under intensive cardiac monitoring.

the interventional radiology team performed a mesenteric
angiogram and initiated an intra-arterial vasopressin
therapy. She had a diverticular bleed that was identified and

was observed and her vasopressin dose had to be increased to
0.2 units per minute.  During this time she did receive
intravenous Nitroglycerin to protect her myocardium and she
was observed for signs and symptoms of both mesenteric and
cardiac ischemia.  At the time of angiography, it appeared
that patient's GI hemorrhage was controlled with the
intra-arterial vasopressin and it was continued at 0.15 units
per minute followed by decrease to 0.1 unit per minute to be
continued through the night.  By the patient's third hospital
day her vasopressin was discontinued.  During this time she

blood cells.  The patient was observed over the following
hospital days for any evidence of re-bleeding.  Over the
ensuing days the patient's hematocrit continued to trend
downward and after she had been transferred from the Medical
Intensive Care Unit she was observed to have another episode
of melena.  The patient was still without a clear source of
bleeding and for this reason her upper endoscopy was
repeated, revealing only gastritis.  She had another tag red
blood cell scan demonstrating bleeding that appeared to
originate from the right colon.  The interventional radiology

similar to the tag red blood cell scan obtained at [**Hospital 8641**]

however, due to the patient's extensive atherosclerotic
mesenteric disease, she was not a candidate for transcatheter
embolization as it put her at an unacceptable risk for bowel
infarction.  In addition, repeat vasopressin therapy was also

that she be prophylaxed with antibiotics against bacterial

initiated on total parenteral nutrition therapy.  During her

the patient was able to start clear liquid and was advanced

melenic blood.  However, patient had a large colonic

concerned presently about the status of her bowel movements.

diet of soft solids in addition to Boost supplements and her
total parenteral nutrition was discontinued.  Plan was
initiated to transfer the patient back to her nursing home.

patient's primary care physician as to whether or not she is
suitable to return to the level of care provided by her
nursing home or if she instead requires a brief stay at the
rehabilitation aspect of [**Hospital 2670**] Nursing Home.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:  Aricept 5 mg po q day, Ritalin 5 mg
po q day, Effexor XR 37.5 mg po q day, Digoxin 0.125 mg po q

patient does take a variety of other medications including

has not needed to be diuresed during her postoperative stay.

diet, she may need further cardiac pharmacological
intervention.  On [**2144-8-27**], the patient was transferred back
to [**Hospital 2670**] Nursing Home in [**Location (un) 8641**], [**Location (un) 3844**], for
further management and care.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
1.  Right colonic diverticular bleeding, now status post
angiography and attempted vasopressin therapy and status post
right colectomy with reanastomosis.

verapamil dose with some elevated blood pressures during her
hospital stay, and was asked to with in the range of 140s to
150s and told to followup with her outpatient physician
regarding adjusting her medication.

oxygen less than home requirements.  Home with VNA services.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:

2. Tracheobronchomalacia.

9. Advair Diskus 250/50 one puff b.i.d.

with severe congestive heart failure with an ejection

Upon arrival to [**Hospital1 69**]
Emergency Department, the patient initially had an oxygen
saturation of 93% while being bagged with 100% FIO2.  She was
given lasix intravenously x 2, aspirin, additional 2 mg of
morphine, and intravenous nitroglycerin was initiated.  She
was started on CPAP 10 and 5 with improvement of her
shortness of breath.  At that time, her chest pain also
resolved.  An arterial blood gas was done, which showed
7.30/51/440.

She was then admitted to the [**Hospital Ward Name 516**] Intensive Care Unit
for respiratory and cardiovascular monitoring.

Her past cardiac history includes a transthoracic
echocardiogram in [**2146-8-17**], which showed an ejection
fraction of less than 15%, severely depressed left
ventricular function, severe global left ventricular
hypokinesis, normal right ventricular wall motion, and 2+

duration.

1.  Appendectomy

4.  Cesarean section x 3

widow.  She lives by herself in [**Location 1268**].  She
occasionally has visiting nurse assistance.

mg once daily, Lipitor 10 mg once daily, Synthroid 0.1 once

13.2, hematocrit 37.6, platelets 33.2.  PT 13.7, PTT 28.1,

was negative.  Chest x-ray showed cardiomegaly with worsening
interstitial edema as compared to previous admission.
Admission electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm, left atrial
enlargement, left bundle branch block, with no change
compared to previous electrocardiograms.

PERTINENT STUDIES DURING ADMISSION:
1.  Transthoracic echocardiogram dated [**2147-7-26**]:  Ejection
fraction less than 20%, left ventricular systolic function
severely depressed, dyskinetic apex, inferior wall thin and
akinetic, right ventricular free wall hypokinesis, 3+ mitral
regurgitation, no effusion.
2.  Cardiac catheterization dated [**2147-7-28**]:  Two vessel
coronary artery disease with normal left main coronary
artery, 90% lesion in left anterior descending, 90% lesion in
circumflex, with dominant right coronary artery with no
significant disease.
3.  Transthoracic echocardiogram dated [**2147-8-8**]:  Ejection
fraction less than 20%, severe regional left ventricular
systolic dysfunction, dyskinetic apex, basal inferior and
inferolateral walls severely hypokinetic, remaining walls
akinetic, focal hypokinesis in apical free wall of right
ventricle, 2+ mitral regurgitation.
4.  Bronchoscopy dated [**2147-8-9**]:  Left airways, upper, lingual
and lower, all segments patent, with frothy, thin secretions.
No plugs noted.

HOSPITAL COURSE TO DATE:
1.  Congestive heart failure:  The patient was admitted
[**2147-7-22**] to [**Hospital Ward Name 516**] Intensive Care Unit for congestive
heart failure exacerbation.  Her presentation was very
similar to her last four admissions over the last five
months.  She was diuresed aggressively.  She was ready for
discharge on hospital day number two when it was noted that
she was in first degree AV conduction delay.  She was
transferred to the [**Hospital Ward Name 517**] Coronary Care Unit on [**2147-7-24**]
secondary to arrhythmias (see below).

Upon admission to the Coronary Care Unit, she immediately
became short of breath, complained of chest pain, was
tachycardic to 120s, later followed by bradycardia down to
the 30s.  She became progressively tachypneic, with
desaturations, and she was electively intubated.  At the
time, it was thought that she was having acute (flash)
pulmonary edema.  She was extubated after two days, on
[**2147-7-26**], however, was reintubated the following day on
[**2147-7-27**] secondary to shortness of breath, chest pain and
tachypnea.

She was taken for cardiac catheterization on [**2147-7-28**] (see
below), and a Swan was placed for hemodynamic monitoring.  It
was noted that her PA diastolic pressures were elevated to
the 40s.  She was continued on aggressive diuresis.
Transthoracic echocardiogram on [**7-26**] showed an ejection
fraction of 20% with a follow-up echocardiogram on [**8-8**] after
revascularization which was unchanged.

Between [**7-28**] and [**8-1**], numerous attempts were made to
wean the patient to pressure support ventilation and each
time failed due to desaturations and tachypnea.  She was
extubated for the second time on [**2147-8-2**], but reintubated
within 45 minutes secondary to tachycardia to 150s,
ventricular fibrillation, desaturations to 80% while on face
[**Last Name (LF) **], [**First Name3 (LF) **] agitation.  Although at that time she had been
aggressively diuresed with appropriate response in her PA
diastolic pressures, it was thought that she still was volume
overloaded, and reintubations were secondary to flash
pulmonary edema.  Therefore, she was further diuresed and
extubated for a third time on [**2147-8-5**].  At the time of
extubation, she was immediately bridged to noninvasive
pressure support ventilation (BiPAP), and continued further
diuresis.

On [**2147-8-6**], while on BiPAP, she had another episode of
tachycardia, hypotension and respiratory distress.  She was
stabilized on fentanyl and Versed, with an esmolol drip, when
it was found that her tachycardia was secondary to atrial
fibrillation.  Although she avoided reintubation that night,
her atrial fibrillation continued for eight hours, and she
spontaneously converted to normal sinus rhythm the following
morning.

After the atrial fibrillation event, she was stabilized and
taken off BiPAP and placed on nasal cannula, which she
tolerated without event for greater than 24 hours.  On
[**2147-8-7**], after being extubated for approximately three days,
she was transferred to the floor.  Later that evening, she
again desaturated to the 80s, had another episode of flash
pulmonary edema, and was reintubated.  She was then taken
back to the Coronary Care Unit.

At the time of that episode, the patient was net negative
greater than 5 liters since the Swan-Ganz catheter was
pulled, showing a PA diastolic of around 15 to 20.  Although
it appeared that she had been aggressively diuresed, further
diuresis was continued, and she was extubated again [**2147-8-10**].
She was continued on BiPAP during the following days, with
intermittent use of nasal cannula and face [**Month/Day/Year **].  She
tolerated being off BiPAP well until the evening of [**2147-8-12**],
in which she had an episode of chest pain followed by
shortness of breath, again desaturated, was placed back on
BiPAP, and avoided reintubation.

At the time of this dictation, the patient was still
maintained on BiPAP overnight, with face [**Date Range **] and nasal
cannula during the daytime.

2.  Coronary artery disease:  The patient was admitted for a
fifth congestive heart failure exacerbation in less than six
months, which was presumed to be ischemic cardiomyopathy.
Exact diagnosis could not be known, as the patient refused
cardiac catheterization for many years.  Cardiac enzymes were
cycled on admission, and a troponin peaked at 32.4 on [**7-25**],
which occurred after transfer to the Coronary Care Unit and
after her first intubation.  Her CKs only were mildly
elevated, with a peak of 133 and a CK/MB of 9 and an index of
5.2.

The patient initially refused cardiac catheterization on this
admission as well but, after her second intubation, it was
thought that ischemic etiology had to be ruled out, and she
agreed to catheterization on [**2147-7-28**].  Cardiac
catheterization showed a normal left main and right coronary
artery without significant disease, however, the left
anterior descending and left circumflex both had 90% lesions,
which were stented with 0% residual.  An intra-aortic balloon
pump was placed after catheterization, and initially was very
difficult to wean due to dramatic fall in blood pressure.
However, on [**2147-8-2**], the balloon pump was able to be weaned
and pulled without event.

Following catheterization, aspirin and Plavix were initiated,
however, Integrilin was not started secondary to the
patient's age.  ACE inhibitors were initially started, and
Captopril was titrated up to 25, but the patient's blood
pressure did not tolerate.  This was discontinued, and
Lisinopril was started the following week, which was
eventually titrated up to 5 mg once daily and Lopressor at
12.5 twice a day at the time of dictation.

3.  Arrhythmias:  While in the [**Hospital Ward Name 516**] Intensive Care
Unit, the patient was noted to have first degree AV
conduction delay.  Upon transfer to the [**Hospital Ward Name 517**], she was
found to be in third degree AV block/high-grade
intraventricular conduction delay.  She was immediately
transferred to the Coronary Care Unit and intubated as above.
Initially the third degree block/intraventricular conduction
delay was thought to be secondary to supratherapeutic Digoxin
levels (2.5), and a transvenous pacer was placed [**2147-7-24**],
however, the patient did not require pacing until
post-catheterization, when she had an episode of bradycardia
to the 50s, and ventricular pacing was initiated.

Although her conduction delay was initially thought to be
secondary to medications, her difficulty in extubation was
attributed to loss of atrial kick.  Therefore, a decision was
made to place a dual chamber pacemaker on [**2147-7-31**].  The
patient did well with the pacemaker, and was almost 100%
captured, with few exceptions.  One notable exception
occurred on [**2147-8-6**], when an episode of paroxysmal atrial
fibrillation occurred, but spontaneously converted eight
hours later.  The patient was maintained on amiodarone
initially at 400 mg twice a day, which was weaned down to 400
once daily, with no other significant arrhythmias at the time
of dictation.

4.  Pulmonary:  Although the difficulty with extubation was
thought to be mainly secondary to congestive heart failure
and very low ejection fraction, Pulmonary was consulted for
recommendations.  The Pulmonary team also believed that the
patient's difficulty with extubation was secondary to
congestive heart failure, but was concerned about a left
lower lobe collapse as seen on chest x-ray.  A bronchoscopy
was performed, which showed no collapsible airways, and some
frothy secretions.  A bronchoalveolar lavage was performed,
which was found to be negative.  Her left lower lobe
atelectasis was treated with incentive spirometer and
pressure support ventilation.

During the hospital course, a history of Guillain-[**Location (un) **]
disease was elicited from the family.  Although the patient
had the disease more than one year ago, pulmonary mechanics
were performed while intubated, and the patient was shown to
have a vital capacity of 1 liter, tidal volume 420.  After
her extubation on [**2147-8-10**], she was continued on BiPAP at
night, and nasal cannula and face [**Date Range **] during the day.  At
the time of dictation, her saturations remained in the high
90s with PO2 above 100, and she was net 8.5 liters negative
since the Swan was pulled, showing a PA diastolic of 15 to
20.  The plan was to continue aggressive diuresis to prevent
further flash pulmonary episodes.

5.  Infectious Disease:  The patient was treated for
enterococcus sensitive to ampicillin and Klebsiella sensitive
to Cipro during her hospital course.  She completed a 12 day
regimen.  There was some concern at the beginning of the
hospital course in which the patient had a high cardiac
output and index and a decreased SVR by Swan-Ganz, which
raised the question of sepsis.  Blood cultures x 4 were all
negative.  Lines were changed frequently, and finally a PICC
line was placed [**2147-8-11**] for long-term intravenous access.

6.  Hematology:  The patient was transfused two units of
packed red blood cells throughout the hospital course, as
well as two units of fresh frozen plasma prior to pacemaker
placement.

7. Renal:  Creatinine bumped only slightly throughout the
hospital course, despite aggressive diuresis.  The plan at
the time of this dictation was to diurese until the patient's
creatinine bumped slightly above 1.2 while still avoiding
acute tubular necrosis.

8.  Fluids, electrolytes and nutrition/gastrointestinal:  A
swallow study was performed [**2147-8-11**] after being extubated two
days, and the patient was found able to tolerate regular thin
liquid diet.

DISPOSITION:  At the time of dictation, the patient still
remains in the Intensive Care Unit, although long-term plans
will be to transfer to the floor with an extensive
rehabilitation facility stay.  Multiple family discussions
were held during the hospitalization, with the most recent
one [**2147-8-11**] in which the patient herself had decided that, if
the need arose, she would like to be reintubated and, if a
long-term tracheostomy needed to be placed, she was agreeable
to this as well.

A follow-up dictation will be provided to summarize the
remainder of the hospital course.

Department he was febrile to 102 and somewhat hypotensive

saturation at 95% on 3 liters and a chest x-ray was

[**Month (only) 216**] of last year a catheterization showed a 70% occlusion
of proximal D1 and a 60% occlusion of proximal obtuse
marginal one, several occluded diagonal and marginal
branches.  He was not felt to be a candidate for intervention

of transient ischemic attack for which he takes Plavix,

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS FOLLOWING LEG BYPASS / THROMBECTOMY
SURGERY

.

This information is designed as a guideline to assist you in a
speedy recovery from your surgery. Please follow these
guidelines unless your physician has specifically instructed you
otherwise. Please call our office nurse if you have any
questions. Dial 911 if you have any medical emergency.

.

ACTIVITY:

.

There are no specific restrictions on activity. You should be as
active as is comfortable. Some fatigue is expected for the first
several weeks. Leg swelling is typical following this type of
surgery and can be controlled by elevating your leg above the
level of your heart when you are not walking. Resume driving
when you are comfortable without the need for pain medication.

.

PLEASE CALL US IMMEDIATELY FOR ANY OF THE FOLLOWING PROBLEMS:

.

Redness in or drainage from your leg wound(s).

.

New pain, numbness or discoloration of your foot or toes.

.

Watch for signs and symptoms of infection. These are: a fever
greater than 101 degrees, chills, increased redness, or pus
draining from the incision site. If you experience any of these
or bleeding at the incision site, CALL THE DOCTOR.

.

Exercise:

.

Limit strenuous activity for 4 weeks.

.

No heavy lifting greater than 20 pounds for the next 7 days.

.

Resume driving when you are comfortable without the need for
pain medication .

BATHING/SHOWERING:

.

You shower immediately upon coming home. No bathing. A clear
dressing may cover your leg incision and this should be left in
place for three (3) days. Remove it after this time and wash
your incision(s) gently with soap and water. Dissolving sutures,
which do not have to be removed, were probably used.

.

If you have staples these will be removed on your follow-up
appointment.

.

WOUND CARE:

.

Sutures / Staples may be removed before discharge. If they are
not, an appointment will be made for you to return for
removal.).

.

When the sutures / staples are removed the doctor may or may not
place pieces of tape called steri-strips over the incision.
These will stay on about a week and you may shower with them on.
If these do not fall off after 10 days, you may peel them off
with warm water and soap in the shower.

.

Avoid taking a tub bath, swimming, or soaking in a hot tub for
two weeks after surgery.

.

MEDICATIONS:

.

Unless told otherwise you should resume taking all of the
medications you were taking before surgery. You will be given a
new prescription for pain medication, which can be taken every
three (3) to four (4) hours only if necessary.

.

Remember that narcotic pain meds can be constipating and you
should increase the fluid and bulk foods in your diet. (Check
with your physician if you have fluid restrictions.) If you feel
that you are constipated, do not strain at the toilet. You may
use over the counter Metamucil or Milk of Magnesia. Appetite
suppression may occur; this will improve with time. Eat small
balanced meals throughout the day.

.

CAUTIONS:

.

NO SMOKING! We know you've heard this before, but it really is
an important step to your recovery. Smoking causes narrowing of
your blood vessels which in turn decreases circulation. If you
smoke you will need to stop as soon as possible. Ask your nurse
or doctor for information on smoking cessation.

.

Avoid bending for 4-6 weeks.

.

No strenuous activity for 4-6 weeks after surgery.

.

DIET :

.

There are no special restrictions on your diet postoperatively.
Poor appetite is expected for several weeks and small, frequent
meals may be preferred.

.

For people with vascular problems we would recommend a
cholesterol lowering diet: Follow a diet low in total fat and
low in saturated fat and in cholesterol to improve lipid profile
in your blood. Additionally, some people see a reduction in
serum cholesterol by reducing dietary cholesterol. Since a
reduction in dietary cholesterol is not harmful, we suggest that
most people reduce dietary fat, saturated fat and cholesterol to
decrease total cholesterol and LDL (Low Density Lipoprotein-the
bad cholesterol). Exercise will increase your HDL (High Density
Lipoprotein-the good cholesterol) and with your doctor's
permission, is typically recommended. You may be self-referred
or get a referral from your doctor.

.

If you are overweight, you need to think about starting a weight
management program. Your health and its improvement depend on
it. We know that making changes in your lifestyle will not be
easy, and it will require a whole new set of habits and a new
attitude. If interested you can may be self-referred or can get
a referral from your doctor.

.

If you have diabetes and would like additional guidance, you may
request a referral from your doctor.

.

FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENT:

.

Be sure to keep your medical appointments. The key to your
improving health will be to keep a tight reign on any of the
chronic medical conditions that you have. Things like high blood
pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol are major villains to
the blood vessels. Don't let them go untreated!

.

Please call the office on the first working day after your
discharge from the hospital to schedule a follow-up visit. This
should be scheduled on the calendar for seven to fourteen days
after discharge. Normal office hours are 8:30-5:30 Monday
through Friday.

.

PLEASE FEEL FREE TO CALL THE OFFICE WITH ANY OTHER CONCERNS OR
QUESTIONS THAT MIGHT ARISE.
